target.title: Machine translation of cortical activity to text with an encoder–decoder framework
target.version: Author manuscript; final edited form published April 2020

read.pdf: Fig. 1–7 and Table 1 (captions/table transcription in text.txt; no separate PDF supplied)

entries.text: The proposed sequence-to-sequence RNN encodes sentence-length ECoG activity and decodes English text word by word, adapting a machine-translation framework to speech decoding.
entries.condition: Sentence-level ECoG input; English sentence output.
entries.quote: we train a recurrent neural network to encode each sentence-length sequence of neural activity into an abstract representation

entries.text: The network is supervised with transcriptions of participants' spoken sentences; its basic labeled output elements are words rather than phonemes.
entries.condition: Participants read prompted sentences aloud; output tokens are words and an end-of-sequence token.

entries.text: ECoG was recorded from implanted grids in peri-Sylvian cortex while participants read sentences aloud during clinical seizure monitoring.
entries.condition: Clinical epilepsy monitoring; prompted aloud reading; cortical ECoG.

entries.text: The abstract describes approximately 250 electrodes per participant.
entries.condition: ECoG grids over peri-Sylvian cortices; participant-specific electrode counts vary (the Methods report 256-channel grids for three and a 128-channel grid for one).
entries.loc: Abstract; Methods, Data collection and preprocessing

entries.text: The implanted ECoG grids had 4-mm pitch.
entries.condition: High-density peri-Sylvian ECoG grids used during sentence reading.

entries.text: The input feature is the z-scored analytic-amplitude envelope of high-γ ECoG, derived from eight adjacent bands spanning 70–150 Hz; bipolar referencing is used.
entries.unit: Hz band; Hz feature sampling rate
entries.condition: Eight adjacent frequency bands are averaged; analytic amplitudes are z-scored on a 30-s sliding window; participants c and d are sampled at about 190 Hz rather than 200 Hz.

entries.text: Four female, right-handed, left-hemisphere language-dominant participants with epilepsy contributed data; ages were 47, 31, 29, and 49 years.
entries.condition: All were undergoing epilepsy treatment and clinical ECoG monitoring; data collection and analysis were not blind to experimental conditions.

entries.text: MOCHA-TIMIT contains 460 sentences and about 1,800 unique words, administered in blocks of 50 (60 in the final block).
entries.unit: sentences; unique words; sentences per block
entries.condition: Two participants read MOCHA-TIMIT; blocks were repeated as time allowed.

entries.text: The picture-description task comprised 30 sentences, about 125 words, and was read by two participants.
entries.condition: Sentences described three unseen cartoon drawings; blocks contained all 30 or a 10-sentence subset for one picture.

entries.text: Word-level references were manually transcribed or corrected manually after speech-to-text assistance; nonwords and other deviations were mapped to OOV, under 1% of tokens.
entries.unit: % of data tokens mapped to OOV
entries.condition: Actual spoken output could differ from the prompted sentence; decoder used a fixed vocabulary and OOV token.

entries.text: Training jointly minimizes word-sequence cross-entropy and an auxiliary MFCC-prediction loss; predicted MFCCs are discarded at test time.
entries.condition: The paper describes stochastic gradient descent/backpropagation and dropout; MFCC prediction is an auxiliary training objective, not a use-time output.
entries.quote: during testing, the MFCC predictions are simply discarded, and decoding is based entirely on the decoder RNN’s output.

entries.text: Temporal convolution downsamples high-γ input by a factor of 12 to about 16 Hz before a three-layer bidirectional LSTM encoder; the decoder is autoregressive.
entries.unit: downsampling factor; Hz; encoder RNN layers
entries.condition: Convolution filters use width and stride 12; decoder takes the previous true word during training and its previous predicted word during testing.
entries.loc: Secs. Decoding pipeline and Implementation: architecture

entries.text: For MOCHA-TIMIT, the output layer has 1,806 word classes even when training and testing only on MOCHA-1.
entries.condition: MOCHA-1 itself has about 250 unique words; the larger output dimension supports comparisons with cross-task training.
entries.quote: For MOCHA-TIMIT, we let the output dimension be 1,806 even when training and testing only with MOCHA-1

entries.text: At inference, the decoder feeds back its own predicted word; greedy word selection was used and beam search was not used in the reported experiments.
entries.condition: Word-by-word decoding terminates at EOS; no external correction step is described.

entries.text: The decoder learns sentence regularities from a restricted set of prompts; the article does not describe an external language model used during decoding.
entries.condition: Language restricted to 30–50 sentence types; models output words autoregressively.

entries.text: WER is the average over tested sentences of minimum insertions, deletions, and substitutions divided by reference length; it is zero for perfect decoding and unbounded in principle.
entries.condition: Reported WER is sentence-averaged; an empty prediction yields 100% WER.

entries.text: The headline encoder–decoder result is mean WER as low as 3% on a held-out repeat set.
entries.condition: MOCHA-1 test repeats, 50 sentence types and about 250 unique words; one example participant in Fig. 2a, with other participants reported as similar; not novel-sentence testing.
entries.quote: Average word error rates across a held-out repeat set are as low as 3%.

entries.text: The phoneme-based HMM sentence classifier had approximately 33% WER, about an order of magnitude above the encoder–decoder result.
entries.condition: Same held-out MOCHA-1 ECoG blocks and 50-sentence candidate set as the comparison; one HMM per sentence with phoneme-constrained Viterbi decoding.
entries.quote: The WERs for this model, approximately 33% (Fig. 2a, ‘phoneme-based HMM’), are about an order of magnitude larger than that of the encoder–decoder network.

entries.text: The authors cite 60% WER as the previous speech-decoding state of the art, on a smaller 100-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Prior continuous-speech decoding system cited as reference 9; not a matched comparison to the present held-out-repeat protocol.
entries.quote: The previous state-of-the-art WER for speech decoding is 60%, and operated with a smaller (100-word) vocabulary9.

entries.text: Spatially downsampling the grid by discarding every other channel in both dimensions left nominally 64 rather than 256 channels and increased error rates about fourfold.
entries.unit: fold WER increase; channels; mm grid spacing (downsampled; original)
entries.condition: Ablation on the example MOCHA-1 participant; simulated lower-density grid; Fig. 2a.
entries.quote: The error rates are about four times greater—although within the usable range, showing the importance of the algorithm in addition to high-density grids.

entries.text: Removing MFCC supervision worsened error rates several-fold, though the authors describe results as still within the usable range; this matters when audio is unavailable to a speech prosthesis user.
entries.condition: Ablation omits the auxiliary MFCC prediction target during training; ECoG-to-text decoding remains the primary objective.

entries.text: Replacing temporal convolution with a fully connected input layer made WER eightfold higher.
entries.condition: Ablation retrained from scratch on the example participant's MOCHA-1 task; no-convolution model also used smaller mini-batches.
entries.quote: WERs octuple.

entries.text: A length-only control replacing ECoG samples with Gaussian noise had approximately 100% WER and was described as near chance.
entries.condition: Networks retrained from scratch; input sequences retained the correct lengths but contained Gaussian noise; 50 MOCHA-1 sentence classes.
entries.quote: Performance is much worse than that of any of the decoders—indeed, near chance (WERs of about 100%; see ‘length info. only’ box in Fig. 2a).

entries.text: No participant had more than 40 minutes of training data.
entries.condition: Four participants; total training-set duration per participant.

entries.text: With each participant's full training set, participants b and d reached WER below 8%.
entries.condition: Participants b/pink and d/brown on their respective training data; held-out repeat blocks.

entries.text: Participant a had about four minutes of MOCHA-1 data (two passes through all 50 sentences, excluding the held-out block).
entries.condition: Participant a; MOCHA-1 held-out block evaluation.

entries.text: Pretraining participant a's network on participant b's ten MOCHA-1 repeats reduced participant a's WER by about 17%; the paired comparison was significant after correction.
entries.condition: Participant a target with two MOCHA-1 training passes; pretraining on participant b; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
entries.quote: Indeed, this transfer-learning procedure decreases WER by about 17%

entries.text: Training participant a from scratch on two repeats of MOCHA-2 through MOCHA-9 (410 sentences disjoint from MOCHA-1) reduced MOCHA-1 WER by 31% over baseline (P ≪ 0.001).
entries.unit: repeats; unique sentences; % WER decrease; P value
entries.condition: Training on MOCHA-TIMIT blocks 2–9 plus the intended cross-task data; test on held-out MOCHA-1 block(s) for participant a.
entries.quote: This cross-task training decreases WER by 31% over the baseline (from the first to the third box, ‘task TL’, of Fig. 3a; P ≪ 0.001).

entries.text: Dual transfer learning reduced participant a's WER by 36% over baseline, but did not significantly improve on task transfer alone after correction.
entries.condition: Pretraining on participant b's MOCHA-TIMIT data, then training on participant a's MOCHA-TIMIT data, followed by held-out MOCHA-1 evaluation; difference versus task transfer alone not significant after multiple-comparison correction.

entries.text: For participant b trained on only two passes, combining transfer from participant a and sentences outside the test set improved WER by about 36% over baseline (P < 0.005 after correction).
entries.unit: passes; % WER decrease; corrected P value
entries.condition: Participant b; cross-participant pretraining from a plus task transfer using MOCHA-2 through MOCHA-9; MOCHA-1 held-out evaluation.

entries.text: For participant d, adding other MOCHA sentences did not improve results; cross-participant pretraining from b did, while its additional benefit combined with task transfer was not significant after correction.
entries.unit: corrected P value for cross-participant transfer
entries.condition: Participant d; transfer from participant b; test on held-out blocks for participant d.

entries.text: Cross-participant transfer learning did not improve results for the two picture-description participants.
entries.condition: Participants c and d's picture-description task.
entries.quote: Finally, for the two participants reading picture descriptions, participant transfer learning did not improve results.

entries.text: The largest gradient-based electrode contributions were in ventral sensorimotor cortex and superior temporal gyrus; STG coverage was present in three of four participants.
entries.unit: participants with STG coverage; participants total
entries.condition: Electrode-contribution gradients from trained models; participant c lacked STG coverage; bipolar-referenced input.

entries.text: The Fig. 2a and Fig. 3 boxplots summarize 30 independently trained models per condition, evaluated on randomly held-out blocks.
entries.condition: Randomly held-out validation blocks; matched held-out block assignments within a participant for paired decoder comparisons.
entries.quote: each box in Fig. 2a and Fig. 3 shows the average (and its standard error) WER across 30 models trained from scratch

entries.text: The training-data curve in Fig. 2b averages ten independently trained models per point.
entries.condition: Four participants; data points use randomly held-out blocks and show mean WER and mean number of repeats with standard errors.

entries.text: WER folds held out randomly selected blocks (about 10% of data) and trained a fresh network from scratch on the remaining blocks; block randomization was fixed once per participant for paired tests.
entries.unit: % of data held out per evaluation
entries.condition: The held-out unit is a block/repeat, not an unseen sentence type or a held-out participant.
entries.quote: For each evaluation, N randomly chosen blocks were held out for testing

entries.text: Comparisons used one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on matched validation-block pairs and Holm–Bonferroni correction; Fig. 2a used five comparisons and transfer tests used 14.
entries.condition: Model instances were matched by held-out block; model and validation-block randomization was fixed per participant for pairwise comparisons.
entries.quote: The resulting P values were then Holm– Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons.

entries.text: Hyperparameters were selected using one participant (b) and one validation block, and this block was not excluded from the final tests; the authors considered it about one tenth of test size and unlikely to leak information.
entries.unit: participant; fraction of total test size represented by the reused block
entries.condition: Participant b/pink; single validation block used during ad hoc tuning and grid search.

entries.text: The minimum number of participants and number of model instances were not selected using statistical power methods.
entries.condition: Across-decoder comparisons.

entries.text: The authors cite 5% WER as professional-level transcription and 20–25% as the outer bound of acceptable performance.
entries.condition: Reference benchmarks for speech transcription, not thresholds measured in this study.

entries.text: The evaluated language is restricted to 30–50 sentences; the authors say the amount of data needed to expand from these tiny languages to general English remains to be established.
entries.condition: Closed, repeatedly read sentence sets; MOCHA-1 has about 250 unique words and picture descriptions about 125.

entries.text: The decoder frequently substitutes valid phrases or whole sentences from its training set, revealing a strong sentence-set bias that may improve closed-set results.
entries.condition: Restricted language of 30–50 prompted sentences.

entries.text: Task transfer from sentences outside the MOCHA-1 test set improved decoding, which the authors interpret as evidence that the network learns subsentence/word information rather than only classifying sentence identities; novel-sentence generalization is proposed, not directly evaluated.
entries.condition: Cross-task training uses MOCHA-2 through MOCHA-9, disjoint from the MOCHA-1 sentence set; final evaluation remains on MOCHA-1.
entries.quote: it implies that the network has learned to identify words, not just sentences, from ECoG data

entries.text: For a person unable to speak, MFCC targets may be unavailable and omission degrades performance; inference otherwise requires ECoG, target-sentence text, and manually extracted onset/offset times.
entries.condition: Proposed speech-prosthesis use; MFCC predictions are not required at use time.

entries.text: The authors say the decoding stage operates close to real time and propose that chronically implanted participants could supply far more training data; no chronic prosthesis outcome is reported.
entries.condition: Discussion of prospective BMI/speech-prosthesis use, not an evaluated deployment.

entries.text: The authors identify changes in cortical representations caused by impairment or post-impairment plasticity as a likely deployment challenge.
entries.condition: Potential use in people with speech impairment; current data are from clinical epilepsy monitoring participants reading aloud.

entries.text: The authors note that data-driven features are difficult to characterize and that error examples do not reliably reveal the feature space; they defer a thorough feature investigation to future work.
entries.condition: Interpretation of trained neural features and decoder errors.

entries.text: The authors warn that electrode-gradient attribution can be misleading with common-average referencing because activity may be smeared across the grid; their models used bipolar reference.
entries.condition: Anatomical attribution based on gradients of loss with respect to ECoG activity.

entries.text: No random-number-generator seeds are reported for model initialization, random block selection, or training data order; the text reports repeated fits but not seed values.
entries.condition: The paper reports 30 model runs for boxplots and random held-out blocks, but no seed schedule or reproducibility seed is specified.
entries.quote: the randomization of validation blocks was performed just once for each participant, allowing pairings of all 30 model instances for any two decoders under comparison.

entries.text: The paper reports block-held-out evaluation within participants but no participant-held-out test of a decoder on a speaker whose neural data were absent from target training; speaker-independent generalization is therefore unmeasured.
entries.condition: Cross-participant transfer uses source-participant pretraining and target-participant data, then evaluates on target-participant held-out blocks; this is not a held-out-speaker test.
entries.quote: For each evaluation, N randomly chosen blocks were held out for testing, and a network was trained from scratch on the remaining blocks

entries.text: Although blocks were collected across several days, the paper does not state whether training and held-out blocks were separated by recording session/day or whether both partitions could share a session.
entries.condition: Reported resampling unit is blocks; no session-held-out evaluation is described.
entries.loc: Methods, Task; Hyperparameter optimization and cross-validation

entries.text: The high-γ feature z-scoring window is specified as 30 seconds, but the paper does not state whether it is causal/trailing or uses future samples, nor whether its statistics cross train/test block boundaries.
entries.unit: s z-scoring window; window alignment/scope unspecified
entries.condition: Potential online-use and evaluation leakage condition for the per-channel feature normalization.
entries.quote: The amplitudes of the (complex) analytic signal were then z-scored on the basis of a 30-s sliding window, yielding the ‘high-γ’ signals discussed in the main text.

entries.text: The noise-only control is called near chance, but no formal chance baseline or chance calculation for the 50-sentence task is given.
entries.condition: Length-preserving Gaussian-noise inputs; approximately 100% WER reported.

entries.text: The public EFC block-breakdown example maps participant b to subject 401 and marks block 83 as validation and block 87 as testing; this is the concrete configuration, while the paper's reported CV also uses randomly selected held-out blocks.
entries.condition: Example repository configuration only; participant b alias is defined for subject 401 and both blocks are type mocha-1.

entries.text: The public EFC MoCHA configuration sets 800 epochs, feed-forward dropout 0.1, RNN dropout 0.5, EMA decay 0.99, and temporal convolution on; these exact values are absent from the supplied article text.
entries.unit: epochs; FF dropout; RNN dropout; EMA decay; temporal convolution enabled
entries.condition: Repository configuration for participants a–d in the MOCHA word-sequence experiment.

entries.text: The public MoCHA configuration sets beam_width to 1, consistent with single-best/greedy decoding; the article says beam search was not used but does not give this parameter value.
entries.condition: MOCHA word-sequence configuration; decoding output is a word sequence terminated at EOS.

entries.text: The EFC config sets optimizer temperature to 0.384; the public TensorFlow training code computes learning rate as temperature divided by the number of training cases, a schedule/value not given in the supplied article text.
entries.unit: optimizer temperature; learning rate = temperature / training-case count
entries.condition: MOCHA word-sequence run configuration and TensorFlow SequenceNetwork implementation.

entries.text: The public training code shuffles data and draws random temporal offsets without a seed; neither repository sets a seed for these runs (the only seed call is in graphical_models/EFHs.py, unrelated).

questions.q: What exactly is conditioned by the headline 3% WER result?
questions.answer: It is mean WER on held-out repeats of the same MOCHA-1 set: 50 prompted sentence types and about 250 unique words. It is not an open-vocabulary or novel-sentence test; the paper reports one example participant at about 3% and says the other three were similar.

questions.q: Does the study demonstrate generalization to unseen sentences or speakers?
questions.answer: It does not directly test novel-sentence decoding: primary evaluation holds out repeat blocks while retaining the same sentence types. Cross-task transfer on 410 sentences disjoint from MOCHA-1 supports learning subsentence/word information, which the authors interpret as making novel-sentence generalization possible. No participant-held-out evaluation is reported.

questions.q: What limits the clinical speech-prosthesis interpretation?
questions.answer: The evidence comes from four epilepsy-monitoring participants reading aloud from small fixed sentence sets; the evaluation is block-held-out WER, not a chronic prosthesis deployment. Removing the auxiliary audio target worsens performance, and the authors flag impairment-related cortical changes as a likely challenge. Only the decoder stage is described as close to real time.

questions.q: Which earlier work used the same attention encoder-decoder for neural-to-text decoding, and under what test split?
questions.answer: Krishna et al. (arXiv 1908.05743, v1 2019-08) trained an attention RNN encoder-decoder on EEG for 9 or 30 repeated USC-TIMIT sentences with an 80/10/10 split; 70% WER (attention, spoken EEG, T7/T8). Writer grepped the passages directly (Sec. 2.2, Sec. 7).

questions.q: Are the Fig. 2a ablations (64 channels, no MFCC, no convolution) reported for participants other than the example one?
questions.answer: Only in Supplementary Fig. 1; the main text says relative performance for the other three participants is quite similar. Writer grepped Results, Decoding performance and Discussion.

questions.q: Triage: received date of the target?
questions.answer: Not stated in the author manuscript or the PMC XML; PMC gives epub 2020-03-30, ppub 2020-04. Krishna arXiv v1 2019-08 is 7 months earlier (prior by the 6-month rule).
